sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and continuation facts: stop versus yield, crossbuck versus signals, city versus interstate limits, shoulder versus lane closure, guide versus service signs, loops versus spurs, and work zone extras
Confusable pairs among the regulatory, railroad, work zone and guide signs, plus continuation facts that complete part C; each block ties to one guide page, pictures are not described, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec09-R01 | anchor: A01
A stop sign is red with white letters and eight sides, while a yield sign is a triangle in red and white with red letters. [A01]
Why it matters: group regulatory signs; confusable stop versus yield colors and shapes; difficulty high.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-R02 | anchor: A01
A stop sign demands a full stop every time, while a yield sign demands slowing and giving way to traffic already in the intersection or on the road you are entering. [A01]
Why it matters: group regulatory signs; confusable stop versus yield duty; difficulty medium.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-R03 | anchor: A01
A Wrong Way sign means you are already in an oncoming lane, while a Do Not Enter sign at a road opening warns you not to go in at all. [A01]
Why it matters: group regulatory signs; confusable wrong way versus do not enter; difficulty high.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-R04 | anchor: A03
A crossbuck by itself carries a yield duty, while alternately flashing red lights or a lowered gate carry a duty to stop and wait for the train. [A03]
Why it matters: group railroad; confusable yield versus stop at a crossing; difficulty high.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-R05 | anchor: A02
The railroad advance warning sign is round, which sets it apart from the X-shaped crossbuck placed at the crossing itself. [A02]
Why it matters: group railroad; confusable advance sign versus crossbuck; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-R06 | anchor: A02
The 25 mph default applies inside cities, towns and villages, while 40 mph is the floor for normal interstate driving. [A02]
Why it matters: group speed limits; confusable city default versus interstate minimum; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-R07 | anchor: A02
The guide says Missouri has more than 1,300 miles of interstate highway, and lower limits are often posted on urban interstates where interchanges and merging traffic are frequent. [A02]
Why it matters: group speed limits; continuation of interstate limits.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-R08 | anchor: A04
A shoulder work zone asks you mainly to slow down, while a lane closure also asks you to merge into an open lane and drop to the work zone speed limit. [A04]
Why it matters: group work zones; confusable shoulder work versus lane closure; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec09-R09 | anchor: A05
A flagging operation is a fixed site on a two-lane road with flaggers at both ends, while a mobile work zone moves along a travel lane behind a protective vehicle with an arrow panel. [A05]
Why it matters: group work zones; confusable flagging versus mobile; difficulty high.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec09-R10 | anchor: A05
In a mobile work zone, follow the direction shown on the flashing arrow panel and watch for several slow or stopped work vehicles. [A05]
Why it matters: group work zones; continuation of the mobile work zone.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec09-R11 | anchor: A06
Guide signs are green or brown with white lettering, while service signs are blue with white letters or symbols. [A06]
Why it matters: group guide and service signs; confusable colors; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec09-R12 | anchor: A06
Three-digit interstate numbers split by first digit: even means a loop around a city, odd means a spur into it. [A06]
Why it matters: group route signs; confusable loop versus spur; difficulty high.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec09-R13 | anchor: A06
Driving west on an east-west interstate, exit numbers get smaller, and driving south on a north-south interstate, they also get smaller. [A06]
Why it matters: group exit numbers; confusable direction of travel; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec09-R14 | anchor: A06
Plan a trip with a highway map and follow the route signs along the way so you do not get lost. [A06]
Why it matters: group route signs; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec09-R15 | anchor: A03
Common work zone signs include Road Work Ahead, Fresh Oil, Loose Gravel and Right Lane Closed Ahead. [A03]
Why it matters: group work zones; glossary work zone sign text.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-R16 | anchor: A04
Missouri roads have several kinds of work zones, and knowing them helps you predict what you will meet as you drive through. [A04]
Why it matters: group work zones; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec09-R17 | anchor: A03
Be extremely careful whenever work zone signs appear, because some kind of work is going on on the roadway or beside it. [A03]
Why it matters: group work zones; continuation of work zone conduct.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-R18 | anchor: A06
The guide pictures an Authorized Safety Inspection Station sign among the guide and service signs. [A06]
Why it matters: group service signs; picture caption only.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0056]
